rv.q: Aside from a few clanging scenes, it’s a gorgeously executed celebration of a pained subject’s artistry.

Nevertheless, the creative team’s painstaking work has resulted in a riveting, adrenaline rush of a show, propelled by remarkable dancing and a mesmerizing central performance by Myles Frost as the sleek, soft-spoken pop megastar.
They won't be disappointed by MJ.
It's certainly worth seeing, but it's not special — even with a book by two-time Pulitzer Prize winner Lynn Nottage.
The show is at its best when it simply lets Jackson's music speak for itself, delivered by a cast that can more than handle the vocal and physical demands of his catalog.
While 'MJ' succeeds as a celebration of Jackson's artistry and features phenomenal performances, it sidesteps the more troubling aspects of the pop icon's life.

And yet — you knew that was coming, didn’t you? — for all its surface flash and stylish presentation, “MJ” comes across, like most jukebox/bio-musical hybrids, as superficial fan-bait: a glossy but unrevelatory moonwalk through the ups and downs (mostly the ups) of Jackson’s career.
The show is a slick, professionally mounted tribute that will satisfy Jackson's devoted fans, but it doesn't dig deep enough to reveal the complex humanity of its subject.

Even the combined power of Jackson’s material and Wheeldon’s reanimation of it cannot make up for the emptiness at its center; we cannot understand or accept the main character if he’s deliberately kept from us.

It’s also a discomfiting experience, in both what’s obviously left off-stage (this is a commercial Broadway musical which ejected a Variety reporter for asking cast about the allegations at the premiere) and its portrayal of Michael Jackson as a lonely Peter Pan in turmoil.
I left the theater entertained, but not convinced I had really seen the man in the smoke and mirrors.
But logic has little to do with "MJ."
The sequence is novel, invigorating and smart — exactly what the rest of “MJ” isn’t.
Only the music and movement in MJ work — the show’s Michael, Myles Frost, glides and hip-rocks through a physical impersonation that operates above and beyond the show’s own ugly logic.
MJ is the platinum standard the often uninspired, generic jukebox musical could benefit to emulate.
MJ comes as close as any musical that has appeared on a Broadway stage in a very long time.

That’s a transition, not since equaled, that director-choreographer Christopher Wheeldon, book write Lynn Nottage and an impeccable cast led by the star-is-born Myles Frost, bring to pulse-quickening life on the stage.
MJ is a strange experience, at once dazzling and unsatisfying, a peerless display of pizzazz with nothing underneath.
For everything else, MJ The Musical is a thriller.
The difference with “MJ” is that it celebrates a suspected pedophile’s life and not only ignores his crimes but whitewashes them.
You'll leave the Theatre (where the show opens tonight) both on a giddy high from Jackson's music but also grappling with what was and wasn't incorporated.
It’s a credit to everyone involved in MJ, then, that there’s no shortage of joy here.
As it turns out, MJ is both wonderfully fun and predictably blinkered.
But as Jackson says in the second act, “We have the icing, but it doesn’t mean anything unless the cake tastes good,” and no amount of frosting could make this amoral mud pie any easier to swallow.
This is a slickly corporate, officially sanctioned slice of legacy clean-up.
And the barrage of heavily rhythmic songs, accompanied by the onslaught of Jackson-style movement, tends to blend together and teeter on tiresomeness.

Set in the rehearsal hall for Jackson’s 1992. Dangerous World Tour, the story follows two documentarians, one is “Alejandro” played exactingly by GABRIEL RUIZ, who are allowed entre into press-weary Michael’s inner sanctum to chronical his creative process.
But more than anything, it wants us to worship the “King of Pop” as the musical royalty he will always be, no matter what.
It also (much like Michael Jackson himself) comes at a price, and one that the producers weren’t willing to acknowledge, perhaps out of fear of hurting their own commercial success.
Taken as an entertainment MJ satisfies immensely, but as drama not so much.
Perhaps that is what the estate actually wanted; to rejuvenate its coffers by sending audiences thirsting for the real thing.
